agibot-x2.segment: Mid-size humanoid for reception and performances
agibot-x2.tagline: 131 cm humanoid for reception and performances
agibot-x2.summary: AGIBOT X2 (known in China as Lingxi X2) is a mid-size bipedal humanoid robot, about 131 cm tall and weighing 35–39 kg, with 30 degrees of freedom (DoF). It is designed for reception, performances and interaction with people. The X2 Neo is sold on the maker's online store for US$25,600, while the X2 Ultra, which adds LiDAR, a depth camera and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX board, is priced in Thailand at 1,799,000 baht through VST ECS.
agibot-x2.background: AGIBOT was founded in Shanghai in February 2023 by former Huawei engineers and, according to Omdia, was the world's largest shipper of humanoid robots in 2025, with more than 5,100 units and a share of about 39%. The company unveiled the X2 on 11 March 2025 and began official sales in May 2025 in three versions (interactive, Pro and Ultra), priced at about CNY 100,000 to CNY 400,000. In March 2026 AGIBOT reached a total of 10,000 robots produced. In Thailand, AGIBOT announced a partnership with the GULF group to set up a joint venture in March 2026, and held a launch with VST ECS in Bangkok on 25 June 2026, where the X2 was described as the best-selling model. On 17 July 2026 an X2 demonstrated Muay Thai moves in front of the Thai Prime Minister during a visit to AGIBOT's headquarters in Shanghai.
agibot-x2.availabilityNote: VST ECS (Thailand) Co., Ltd. has been AGIBOT's partner and distributor in Thailand since June 2026. It has announced a baht price for the X2 Ultra, has a local training and after-sales service team, and offers outright sales, short-term rental for events and an annual subscription. The X2 Neo can be ordered from AGIBOT's online store, but buyers must ask the sales team about shipping to Thailand.

agibot-a2.segment: Human-size humanoid for reception and customer service
agibot-a2.tagline: 169 cm humanoid for reception and guided tours
agibot-a2.summary: AGIBOT A2 (known in China as Yuanzheng A2) is a human-size bipedal humanoid robot, 169 cm tall and weighing 63–69 kg, designed for reception, exhibition tours and customer information. The A2 Ultra has dexterous hands, camera and LiDAR perception and an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin computer, and is priced in Thailand at 3,118,000 baht through VST ECS. The A2 Lite, intended for performances, is priced at US$44,560 on the maker's online store.
agibot-a2.background: AGIBOT unveiled the A2 in August 2024, and the company began mass production of robots in December 2024. The A2 is currently sold as the A2 Ultra and the A2 Lite, in addition to the wheeled A2-W. The maker states that more than 1,000 A2 Ultra units are already in real-world use, that it has passed 5,100 hours of continuous walking tests, and that it undergoes 92 quality checks to automotive-grade manufacturing standards. In November 2025 an A2 walked 106.286 km in 3 days and was recognised with a Guinness World Record. In Thailand, VST ECS launched the A2 Ultra as its flagship model in June 2026 for customer service, retail and healthcare, and stated that it supports 20 languages including Thai, while the GULF group is working with AGIBOT to deploy reception robots in retail stores and financial service branches.
agibot-a2.availabilityNote: VST ECS (Thailand) has been AGIBOT's distributor in Thailand since June 2026 and has announced a baht price for the A2 Ultra, with a local training and maintenance team; complex repairs are supported by engineers from China. The A2 Lite can be ordered from AGIBOT's online store, with the buyer responsible for shipping, customs duty and import duty.

unitree-g1.segment: Mid-size humanoid for research and education
unitree-g1.summary: The Unitree G1 is a mid-size bipedal humanoid robot, about 132 cm tall and weighing about 35 kg, made by Unitree Robotics of Hangzhou, China. The base version has 23 DoF and a swappable battery with a runtime of about 2 hours, and has a starting price of US$13,500 on the maker's online store. It suits universities, research laboratories and demonstrations, although writing your own control programs requires the EDU version.
unitree-g1.background: Unitree launched the G1 in 2024 as the company's second humanoid robot after the H1, and has sold it through its online store since June 2024. The base version is currently priced at US$13,500, excluding taxes and shipping. In September 2026 the online store added the G1 Pro at US$21,500, which a European distributor states has 29 DoF and a maximum knee torque of 120 N·m. On 14 September 2026 the maker launched the G1+, which adds a 2-DoF neck, binocular cameras together with a wide-angle camera, and shoulder and waist motors with 110% higher maximum torque, priced at US$15,000 (CNY 95,000 including tax in China). The G1 EDU research version supports further development, can be configured with 23–43 DoF, and can be fitted with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin compute module and Dex3-1 hands, with the price given by the maker on enquiry. The maker has also released open-source code for training the G1's movement in simulation on Isaac Lab and MuJoCo.
unitree-g1.availabilityNote: Thai dealers such as SIAMBC (storefront in Thawi Watthana district, Bangkok) and MetaXR take orders by quotation, and Systronics Co., Ltd. was named as a Thai distributor in late 2024. Buyers can also order directly from Unitree's online store, but the store states that the G1 is on backorder and buyers must handle customs clearance themselves.

engineai-t800.segment: Full-size humanoid for research, development and demonstrations
engineai-t800.tagline: Adult-size bipedal robot with 450 N·m joint torque
engineai-t800.summary: The EngineAI T800 is a full-size bipedal humanoid robot, 173 cm tall and weighing 75–85 kg depending on the version. Its joints deliver a maximum torque of 450 N·m, and it has a runtime of 3–5 hours per charge. There are 4 versions, from the Basic for demonstrations up to the Pro and Max, which have dexterous hands and LiDAR and support further development. This makes it suitable for research organisations, system developers and show organisers.
engineai-t800.background: EngineAI (众擎机器人) was founded in October 2023 and is headquartered in Shenzhen. The company launched the T800 on 2 December 2025 and put it on sale immediately at a starting price of CNY 180,000, in Basic, Open Source, Pro and Max versions. A few days later, when some questioned whether the launch video used computer graphics, the company released a clip of its CEO letting the T800 kick him for real to confirm its capabilities. In late May 2026 the production base of about 12,000 m² in Honghualing, Shenzhen, began delivering the first batch of T800s; the maker states that it can produce one unit every 15 minutes and that each robot passes 79 quality checks. The overseas prices once shown on the website ranged from US$40,500 to US$80,800, before the maker removed the price table from both its Chinese and English websites in late September 2026.
engineai-t800.availabilityNote: No official EngineAI distributor has yet been found in Thailand. The order button on the maker's website leads to a JD.com store that serves China, so buyers in Thailand must contact EngineAI directly for an export quotation and handle the import themselves. The maker began delivering the first batch in late May 2026.

nao6.segment: Small humanoid for education and research
nao6.tagline: Small humanoid for the classroom and research
nao6.summary: NAO6 is a small bipedal humanoid robot, 57.4 cm tall and weighing 5.48 kg, with 25 degrees of freedom (DoF). It is used for teaching, human–robot interaction research and healthcare applications. The authorised dealer in France prices it at €10,020 including VAT, and it can be programmed both with drag-and-drop blocks in Choregraphe and in Python or C++.
nao6.background: NAO was developed by Aldebaran, a robotics company founded in Paris in 2005 that later became part of SoftBank Robotics. NAO6 is the sixth generation, launched in May 2018 with a faster processor, higher-resolution cameras and larger memory. The maker states that more than 20,000 NAO robots are in use worldwide. After a French court placed Aldebaran under a court-appointed administrator in June 2025, Maxvision of Shenzhen, China, bought its core assets in July 2025 and set up Maxtronics in France on 28 August 2025 to continue developing, selling and providing after-sales service for NAO. Maxtronics is currently developing the next model, NAO7, which has no announced release date. In Thailand, True Robotics, part of the True group, showcased NAO for business applications in 2017.
nao6.availabilityNote: No Thai dealer publishing a selling price for NAO6 has been found yet. Thai buyers can order from an authorised overseas dealer such as Generation Robots in France, which states delivery within 3 weeks and can ship outside the European Union, or request a quotation directly from Maxtronics. The buyer acts as the importer and must handle customs clearance themselves.

limx-luna.segment: Full-size humanoid for performances and experiential events
limx-luna.tagline: 160 cm humanoid for performances and welcoming guests
limx-luna.summary: LimX Luna is a full-size bipedal humanoid robot, 160 cm tall and weighing about 54–56 kg, with 27 degrees of freedom (DoF) in the body. It is designed for performances, dancing and audience interaction in shopping malls, museums and theme parks. Its retail price in China is CNY 298,000, and it has a runtime of about 4 hours with 2 swappable batteries.
limx-luna.background: LimX Dynamics (逐际动力) was founded in Shenzhen in January 2022. Its major investors include Alibaba, JD.com and Lenovo Capital, and it raised a total of US$400 million between February and July 2026. Earlier products include the TRON 1 bipedal robot (2024) and the full-size humanoid Oli (July 2025, starting price CNY 158,000). The company launched Luna on 25 May 2026, positioning it as a commercial performance robot with a female form and a fabric-covered outer shell. Its retail price in China is CNY 298,000, and the first 100 buyers received a CNY 40,000 discount. Luna can learn dance moves from video, and more than 200 units can be controlled together in a synchronised performance.
limx-luna.availabilityNote: LimX Dynamics has taken pre-orders for Luna in China since May 2026 and plans to expand into overseas markets by 2027. In Thailand, the Drone Association Thailand website (droneth.or.th) lists the product for pre-order with pricing by quotation, but no announcement of an official distributor appointment has been found yet. Buyers should therefore contact LimX Dynamics directly to confirm delivery dates.
limx-luna.distributor: Pre-order directly from LimX Dynamics, or enquire through Drone Association Thailand (droneth.or.th)

galbot-g1.segment: Wheeled dual-arm humanoid for retail and warehouses
galbot-g1.tagline: Dual-arm robot on a wheeled base for picking goods
galbot-g1.summary: Galbot G1 is a robot with a humanlike upper body and two arms mounted on an omnidirectional wheeled base. It stands up to 173 cm tall, weighs 92.5 kg and is designed for picking and delivering goods in retail stores, unstaffed pharmacies and warehouses. It has a runtime of 8 hours per charge and is listed on JD.com in China at CNY 699,900 before discounts.
galbot-g1.background: Galbot (银河通用) was founded in Beijing in 2023 by Wang He and first unveiled the G1 in June 2024, then began commercial service in pharmacies and retail. The maker states that its "银河太空舱" (Galaxy Space Capsule) automated store system using the G1 is operating at more than 170 sites in more than 40 cities, and that the G1 has been used in more than 100 quick-commerce retail warehouses 24 hours a day, continuously for more than a year and a half. Baidu Baike states that cumulative deliveries exceeded 1,200 units by 2025. After the G1 appeared on CCTV's Spring Festival Gala in February 2026, nearly 300 units of the JD.com listing were ordered or added to carts in a single night, with a retailer in Suzhou ordering 2 units within 12 minutes. Chinese media reported that the company had raised about CNY 7 billion in total and was valued at more than CNY 20 billion in March 2026.
galbot-g1.availabilityNote: No Galbot distributor has been found in Thailand yet. The purchase channel recommended on the maker's website is JD.com's self-operated store (sold directly by JD), which serves China. Thai buyers therefore need to contact Galbot directly for an export quotation and handle the import themselves.

market.marketContext: 2025 was the first year in which humanoid robots shipped in the tens of thousands. Omdia estimated global shipments at 13,318 units, while IDC estimated about 18,000 units, an increase of about 5–6 times over 2024, with a market value of about US$440 million. Chinese makers held a share of nearly 90%, led by AgiBot and Unitree, while US makers such as Tesla, Figure AI and Agility Robotics each shipped about 150 units. For the first half of 2026, IDC reported shipments of nearly 25,000 units, and TrendForce expects full-year 2026 shipments to exceed 50,000 units. The main buyers are still research and educational institutions, along with exhibitions and reception work, while factory use remains at the pilot stage. Prices continue to trend downwards: for example, Unitree cut the starting price of the R1 from CNY 39,900 to CNY 29,900 in 2026, and there are small models priced below CNY 10,000. In Thailand the market is still at an early stage. The main sellers are VST ECS, AGIBOT's partner in Thailand since June 2026 (starting price 1,799,000 baht), and several Unitree dealers, focusing on educational and research institutions, events, retail, customer service and airports, while AGIBOT has announced plans to set up a joint venture with the GULF group. On the government side, the Board of Investment (BOI) has granted promotion to 10 humanoid-robot component manufacturing projects with total investment of 15,000 million baht since early 2026, and offers the Smart and Sustainable Industry upgrading measure for businesses investing in automation and robotics.

shipments.note: Estimate by Omdia, which put total global shipments in 2025 at 13,318 units; AgiBot's share was about 39%.
Unitree's own figure is more than 5,500 humanoid robots shipped; the difference comes from the way each source counts.
Approximate figure; mostly used within the company.

priceFactors: The number of degrees of freedom (DoF) and the joint actuators are the main cost of a humanoid robot: the more joints and the higher the torque, the higher the price. For example, the standard Unitree G1 has 23 DoF, while the G1 EDU can be expanded to 43 DoF.
Multi-fingered dexterous hands can add a great deal to the price and are often offered only on research and development versions. Many base versions have no grasping hands, or only simple ones.

Onboard computers such as NVIDIA Jetson Orin or Jetson Thor let AI models run on the robot without relying on the cloud, but add cost and power consumption; a single Jetson AGX Thor developer kit alone costs US$3,499.

The sensor suite, such as 3D LiDAR, depth cameras and multiple microphones, determines how well the robot perceives its surroundings and walks around obstacles, so it is another factor behind price differences.

Access to the software development kit (SDK) and to further development means that versions that look identical can differ in price several times over. Some makers allow low-level control programming only on EDU versions and give them a longer warranty, for example 18 months versus 8 months for the standard version.

Body size, payload and battery capacity directly affect the price. A full-size robot about 170 cm tall, such as the AGIBOT A2 Ultra, is priced at 3,118,000 baht in Thailand, higher than the mid-size X2 Ultra, which starts at 1,799,000 baht.
Makers' prices quoted in US dollars or yuan do not include shipping, customs clearance fees or 7% VAT, so the selling price in Thailand also depends on the exchange rate and the method of import.

Local after-sales service, training, spare parts and spare batteries, as well as rental or monthly subscription options (Robot-as-a-Service), are costs that dealers build into their prices in different ways. Compare the whole package of terms, not just the price of the robot.

buyerChecklist.title: See a demonstration before deciding
buyerChecklist.detail: Ask to see or try the model you plan to buy under real operating conditions. Some dealers have a shop or offer on-location demonstrations, and some offer short-term rental so you can try the robot first.

buyerChecklist.title: Check the version and development rights
buyerChecklist.detail: Base and EDU versions may differ in DoF count, onboard computer and SDK access. If you need to program the robot or carry out research, get written confirmation that the version you buy is open for further development.

buyerChecklist.title: Warranty period and service centres in Thailand
buyerChecklist.detail: Warranty periods vary widely, from 6 to 18 months depending on the model. Ask whether repairs can be done in Thailand or the robot must be sent abroad, and how long this takes.

buyerChecklist.title: Spare parts and spare batteries
buyerChecklist.detail: Ask about prices and lead times for batteries, joints and parts that wear quickly, such as feet and hands. As one battery gives a runtime of about 2 hours, a spare battery allows continuous operation.

buyerChecklist.title: Space and safety
buyerChecklist.detail: Bipedal robots can fall during use or testing. Prepare a clear area with a flat, non-slip floor, a keep-out zone for people and, for full-size models, a safety gantry, and check where the emergency stop button is.

buyerChecklist.title: Network and personal data
buyerChecklist.detail: Robots with cameras and microphones capture images and audio of people. Check which servers the data is sent to and whether the robot can be used offline, and prepare a privacy notice under the Personal Data Protection Act if it will be used at business premises.

buyerChecklist.title: Import documents and NBTC certification
buyerChecklist.detail: Buy through a Thai importer that fully completes customs clearance and NBTC radiocommunication equipment certification. If you import the robot yourself, you take on this paperwork and become the importer under the unsafe products liability law.

buyerChecklist.title: User training
buyerChecklist.detail: Check whether the price includes training for operators and system administrators, covering use of the remote control, charging and storing batteries, software updates and handling emergencies.

buyerChecklist.title: Compare buying with renting
buyerChecklist.detail: For events or pilot projects, rental or a monthly subscription may be better value than buying. Before deciding, weigh how often the robot will be used, maintenance costs and how quickly models are replaced.

steps.title: Prepare the space and floor
steps.detail: Set aside a clear area of at least about 3 x 3 m for testing and demonstrations, with a flat, dry, non-slip floor. Lay impact-absorbing rubber mats in the test area and set a safety zone that keeps bystanders away while the robot is moving.

steps.title: Install a safety gantry
steps.detail: Mid-size and full-size bipedal robots should have a safety gantry or lifting hoist for start-up, testing new motions and program development, to prevent damage if the robot falls.

steps.title: Charging point and battery storage
steps.detail: Provide an earthed power socket in a well-ventilated spot away from flammable materials, set aside a separate place for spare batteries, and assign someone responsible for charging in line with the maker's manual.

steps.title: Network
steps.detail: Provide Wi-Fi coverage across the operating area, separate the robot's network from the organisation's main network, and set permissions for access and software updates.

steps.title: Assess risks and appoint operators
steps.detail: Assess the risks of the tasks the robot will perform, appoint trained operators, and check that the emergency stop button and remote control work before every use.

steps.title: Train users and maintainers
steps.detail: Arrange training in switching the robot on and off, charging, basic maintenance and program development (for EDU versions), and ask the dealer to include the training in the sales contract.

steps.title: Insurance and personal data
steps.detail: Inform your insurer so that it can consider cover for property and third-party liability, and put up signs or notices that images and audio are recorded in areas where the robot operates.

incentives: Under the BOI's Smart and Sustainable Industry upgrading measure, existing businesses, whether or not already BOI-promoted, that invest at least 1 million baht (excluding land and working capital) in upgrading with automation or robots receive an exemption from import duty on machinery and a 3-year corporate income tax exemption capped at 50% of the investment.

If the automation or robots invested in have links with the domestic automation industry of at least 30% of the machinery value, the corporate income tax exemption cap rises to 100% of the investment, and spending on AI, machine learning and data analytics can be counted in full as investment. Those interested should check the application deadline and the latest conditions with the BOI before ordering.

The tax measure to support SME digital transformation under Royal Decree (No. 802) of 2026 lets companies with paid-up capital of no more than 5 million baht and revenue of no more than 30 million baht deduct 2 times the expense for software, hardware, smart devices or digital services registered in the digital service catalogue of the Digital Economy Promotion Agency (depa), up to 300,000 baht, for expenses from 24 June 2025 to 31 December 2027. It applies only if the robot or service purchased is in that catalogue.

For those who want to make parts or assemble robots in Thailand: since early 2026 the BOI has granted promotion to 10 humanoid-robot component manufacturing projects with total investment of 15,000 million baht, covering frames, joint control units, arms and fingers.
legalNotes: As of October 2026, Thailand has no law specifically regulating humanoid robots. The draft Artificial Intelligence Act of the Electronic Transactions Development Agency (ETDA) closed for public consultation in August 2026 and is not yet in force, so robot use falls under existing general laws.

Imports must go through Customs Department clearance. Robots classified under HS code 8479.50 (industrial robots) or 8479.89 carry a 0% import duty rate, but small entertainment robots may be classified under other codes that carry duty. Importers should request an advance tariff classification ruling, and must pay 7% VAT, a rate that will be kept until 30 September 2027.

Robots with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or a mobile network module count as radiocommunication equipment and must be certified or covered by a supplier's declaration of conformity (SDoC), according to the category set by the Office of the NBTC. The applicant must be a maker, importer or dealer in Thailand registered with the NBTC.

Using a robot with cameras or microphones for personal benefit or family activities is exempt under Section 4 (1) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2019, but use at business premises requires informing employees and customers of the purpose and providing a privacy notice, setting a data retention period and managing transfers of data to overseas servers. The Office of the Personal Data Protection Committee issued its first AI guidelines in October 2026; they are not legally binding.

The Liability for Damages Arising from Unsafe Products Act 2008 makes the maker, the importer and any seller unable to identify the maker or importer jointly liable to the injured party, who does not have to prove negligence, and the court may award punitive damages of up to 2 times the actual damages. Buying through a Thai importer therefore gives a clearly responsible party, whereas importing yourself makes the buyer the importer.

Employers using robots in the workplace have safety duties under the Occupational Safety, Health and Environment Act 2011 and the Ministerial Regulation on safety concerning machinery, cranes and boilers 2021, and may refer to the international standards ISO 10218 for industrial robots and ISO 13482 for service robots when assessing risks.

Our checks found no mandatory Thai Industrial Standard (TIS) that applies directly to humanoid robots, but accessories such as chargers may fall under mandatory standards depending on their tariff classification. Ask the importer.

Existing property and third-party liability insurance policies may not automatically cover damage caused by robots. Buyers should inform their insurer and extend cover before starting to use a robot in areas where members of the public are present.
